summary: For ages 6–8, teach the disposition of changing your mind when evidence contradicts your prediction: a prediction-breaking surprise is a highly informative result, not a failure. Learners commit a prediction visibly before testing, confront a genuine mismatch, and explicitly update their idea (not the recorded data), while resisting confirmation bias. Builds on separating observation from interpretation.
misconceptions: Thinking a wrong prediction means you failed, rather than that you learned something.
Ignoring, dismissing, or re-reading a result so it seems to fit the original prediction (confirmation bias).
Believing scientists are people who are always right, rather than people who update when wrong.
Changing the RECORDED data to match the prediction instead of changing the idea.
Treating a confirming result as more valuable than a surprising one.
Feeling that admitting 'I changed my mind' is weakness rather than good science.

activities.title: Predict-o-Tron: lock it in, then watch
steps: Face a genuinely counter-intuitive challenge, choosing one setup for this run — e.g. two solid balls (not hollow), one big and heavy, one small and light, released at the same moment from the top of identical ramps (which reaches the bottom first?), OR two objects placed in water (which sinks and which floats?).
Commit your prediction visibly and in a way you cannot quietly retract — say or write 'I predicted the big one', and pin that choice where it stays visible.
Run the test and watch the actual outcome within the setup you chose (e.g. the two solid balls arrive at about the same time, give or take a small difference; or an object floats/sinks unexpectedly).

When the result breaks your prediction, perform an explicit 'update my idea' move within the setup you ran: for the ramp, drag your idea-token from 'the big one is faster' to a new bin you name yourself; for the float test, drag it from 'the big one sinks' to a new idea you name — change the idea, not the data.
Say the sentence frame aloud: 'I predicted X, but I observed Y, so I've changed my mind.'
Collect the surprise as a 'treasure' — keep a shelf/collection of prediction-breaking results you learned from across several challenges.
activities.insight: The mismatch between what I guessed and what happened is not me failing — it is me learning. A surprising result taught me more than a confirming 'I was right' would have.

activities.title: Spot the confirmation-bias move
steps: Across several trials, keep a tally of every result — including the ones that disagreed with your prediction, not just the ones that agreed.
Notice when you only remembered or valued the trials that fit your guess, and name that pull (the 'magnet' that makes you keep only agreeing results).
Decide what the full set of results — including the surprising ones — says about your idea.
activities.insight: There is a strong pull to notice only results that agree with you; a good scientist counts the disagreeing results too and lets the whole evidence decide.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'I was wrong, and that's great'
steps: Talk with an adult or in-role character who asks: 'What did you predict? What happened? So what will you do with your idea now?'
Hear the adult/character share their OWN belief-change story ('I thought the big one would sink — but it floated — so I need a new idea').
Describe aloud how you feel about being surprised and practise treating it as curiosity, not shutdown.
activities.insight: Changing your mind in light of evidence is normal, high-status science — not weakness or embarrassment.

activities.title: Story of a surprise (primer)
steps: Explore a short scene or story of a scientist's 'I thought … but I found …' moment, including a famous 'oops that changed science'.
Pick out the vocabulary: prediction, observation, surprise, changed my mind.
activities.insight: Scientists are people who update when the evidence surprises them, not people who are always right.

activities.title: What should the scientist do? (short reasoning probe)
steps: Read a short scenario: a result did not match the prediction — what should the scientist do?
Choose and justify a response, and spot the confirmation-bias move in a scenario where someone kept only the agreeing results.

Answer probes: 'If you tried it three more times and the big one floated every time, would you keep your first idea or change it? Why?' and 'Which is more useful to a scientist — a result that surprises you or one you already expected? Why?' and 'If you really wanted your prediction to be right, would that change what the marble actually did?'
activities.insight: Strong reasoning treats a surprising result as real information to learn from (change the idea, or re-test to be sure), not a mistake to hide or explain away; wanting a prediction to be true does not change what actually happened.

checkQuestion: You were sure the big marble would sink and the small one would float. You try it — but the big one floats and the small one sinks. That's the opposite of what you thought! What should you do now, and how do you feel about being surprised?
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning treats the surprising result as real information to learn from, not a mistake to hide or explain away: the child says they should change their idea (or test again to be sure) because the evidence didn't match the prediction, and shows that a surprising result is valuable — it tells you something you didn't know. The key is willingness to update the belief in light of the evidence rather than defend the original prediction.
